articles.title: Stop Shipping Search Boxes With a Race Condition
articles.excerpt: Type "react" into a search box, watch it fetch results, then quickly backspace and type "vue" instead. For half a second, the dropdown shows react results under the word vue. Then it corrects itself,…
articles.body: Type "react" into a search box, watch it fetch results, then quickly backspace and type "vue" instead. For half a second, the dropdown shows react results under the word vue . Then it corrects itself, or it doesn't, and either way nobody files a bug report because by the time you'd screenshot it, it's gone. This happened at a filter UI I worked on — product search, nothing exotic, one fetch() call per keystroke. QA flagged it as "occasionally shows stale results, can't reproduce." That phrase should make you suspicious immediately. "Can't reproduce" usually means "reproduces under conditions I'm not controlling for" — and the condition here was network speed, which nobody controls on purpose.

articles.body: WebRequest looks like a normal HTTP client, but MetaTrader blocks every request until the exact base URL is listed under Tools, Options, Expert Advisors. The call also insists on HTTPS for most brokers and builds, and it returns false with a specific error when the whitelist, protocol, or timeout is wrong. Until those pieces are set, your EA never reaches the remote host. What must be true first Open Tools, Options, Expert Advisors. Enable WebRequest for listed URL, then add the base origin such as https://api.example.com with no path. A path only entry often fails. Save and restart the EA after edits. Use HTTPS. Plain HTTP is refused in current builds for safety. Certificates must validate. Pass a timeout in milliseconds. Zero or a tiny value fails under normal latency.

articles.excerpt: Most of my debugging time isn't spent on hard problems. It's spent on small chores: reading a minified API response, checking what's inside a token, converting a timestamp. Here are five of them, what…
articles.body: Most of my debugging time isn't spent on hard problems. It's spent on small chores: reading a minified API response, checking what's inside a token, converting a timestamp. Here are five of them, what's actually going on in each, and the quickest way to handle them. 1. Reading minified JSON An API returns one 4,000-character line and you need to find one field. Pretty-printing it makes the structure obvious, and validating it tells you where a malformed payload breaks. Common causes of "Unexpected token" errors: A trailing comma after the last item Single quotes instead of double quotes Unquoted keys An HTML error page returned where you expected JSON (the error usually points at the first < ) A formatter shows the exact line and character of the error.

articles.title: One Shared Board for the Whole Household: What Building TaskFamily Taught About Family Software

articles.body: Most household software fails for a reason that has little to do with code quality. A household is a group of people with different schedules, different comfort with technology, and different ideas about what counts as finished. A shared board has to work for the person who checks it every morning and for the person who opens it only when something is missing. TaskFamily began as an attempt to put chores, schedules, lost items, and reminders in one place, instead of spreading them across notes, chats, calendars, and memory. The idea was straightforward: when every household commitment lives in one visible place, fewer commitments fall through the cracks.

articles.title: Why Stateless AI Fails at SRE (And How Contextual Memory Fixes It)
articles.excerpt: During a P1 production outage, every minute of downtime costs thousands of dollars. Standard AI assistants lack organizational context, providing generic textbook advice or hallucinating destructive C…
articles.body: During a P1 production outage, every minute of downtime costs thousands of dollars. Standard AI assistants lack organizational context, providing generic textbook advice or hallucinating destructive CLI commands. To solve this, I built NerveCenter, an intelligent SRE agent that replaces generic AI with historically grounded runbooks. NerveCenter uses Streamlit, Groq (gpt-oss-120b), and Vectorize Hindsight as a dynamic memory layer. When a "Redis OOM Error" alert fires, NerveCenter queries the vector database for similar past incidents. It retrieves Incident 892, outputs the exact redis-cli FLUSHALL ASYNC command used to fix it, and injects the post-mortem notes directly into the context.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star'
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova later caleld the Tycho supernova with his bare eyes. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago.

articles.title: What's that bright 'star' in the early morning sky? It's not a star at all!
articles.excerpt: Spotted a dazzling light in the eastern sky before sunrise? It's Venus, and the planet is only going to get brighter as it heads toward its spectacular peak later this month.
articles.body: Early morning risers heading to work or school before sunrise are likely to notice a very bright, star-like object appearing low in the east-southeast sky just before sunrise. What is somewhat amazing is that just a couple of weeks ago this object wasn't there at all, but now it literally stands out with such brilliance as to almost command the attention of commuters who might be traveling in an easterly direction to "Look at me!" The object in question is, of course, the planet Venus, which is currently amid one of its most spectacular forays into the morning sky, literally "vaulting up" into prominence. On Oct. 24, Venus came to inferior conjunction, passing between the Earth and sun and shifting from the evening into the morning sky.

articles.title: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers

articles.body: Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information—including names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens—for all of its users following a breach of its network security. The accomplishment could be a major coup for the attackers. Both Chainalysis and public sources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It's unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats. We regret to inform you...

articles.excerpt: The Unistellar Envision smart binoculars have an augmented reality (AR) overlay that provides smart functionality to 10x50 binoculars, enabling night sky and landmark identification.
articles.body: I have been waiting to get my hands on a pair of Unistellar Envision smart binoculars since they were announced in 2024. Our editor-in-chief tried an early demo of them last year and said that they felt like something out of Star Trek . He was, of course, referencing the red augmented reality (AR) overlay in the Envisions that can identify night sky targets and landmarks, as well as displaying navigational tools. These are the first pair of smart binoculars that can identify targets in the night sky, such as planets, stars and deep space objects. The build is solid and while they aren't the most lightweight binoculars , the body is hiding that extra technology that enables the AR overlay in the right hand lens.
